engine: markdown
title: "rush plot"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'tibble::rownames_to_column(mtcars, "model")'
rush run -o mpg.csv 'ggplot2::mpg'
rush run -o economics.csv 'ggplot2::economics_long'
rush run -o faithfuld.csv 'ggplot2::faithfuld'
```

The `plot` command builds a [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) graphic
from your data. Choose columns with `--x`, `--y`, `--color`, and friends, and a
sensible geom is guessed for you (override it with `--geom`). The plot is drawn
right in your terminal, or saved as an image.

The examples on this page use two data sets from R: `mtcars` (32 cars, with
their `model` name as a column) and ggplot2's `mpg` (fuel economy of 234 cars).

## Usage

```bash
rush plot [options] [--] [<file>...]
```

## Output

Where the plot goes depends on `--output` (`-o`), `--output-format` (`-O`), and
whether standard output is a terminal:

| You run                         | You get                                        |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `rush plot ...` in a terminal   | ANSI art, in color                             |
| `rush plot ... > file`, or a pipe | PNG bytes                                    |
| `-O ansi` or `-O ascii`         | ANSI art, or plain ASCII art without colors    |
| `-O svg`, `-O pdf`, ...         | That format, on standard output                |
| `-o plot.png`                   | A file, its format inferred from the extension |

Here's the same plot in each of the three main formats.

### ANSI

In a terminal, `rush` draws the plot with colored characters using
[devoutansi](https://github.com/jeroenjanssens/devoutansi):

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv mpg.csv
```

This is the quickest way to look at your data, and works over SSH too.

### ASCII

`-O ascii` draws with plain characters and no escape codes, so the output can
be pasted into an email, a code comment, or a text file:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv -O ascii mpg.csv
```

### PNG

`-o` saves the plot as an image:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv -o displ-hwy.png mpg.csv
```

![](displ-hwy.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of highway mileage against engine displacement, colored by drive type, in the mpg data set" width="560"}

In the terminal, `rush` uses a minimal theme without grid lines, which works
better with characters. Images keep the default ggplot2 theme. (When you pass
`--post`, the terminal keeps your theme too.)

### `--output` (`-o`)

The format follows from the file extension. Any format that
[`ggsave()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html) supports
works, such as `.png`, `.jpeg`, `.pdf`, and `.svg`:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv -o displ-hwy.svg mpg.csv
```

![](displ-hwy.svg){fig-alt="The same scatter plot as an SVG image" width="560"}

Use `-o -` to write to standard output, just as without `-o`.

### `--output-format` (`-O`)

Without `--output`, `rush` writes ANSI art to a terminal and PNG bytes to
anything else, such as a file or a pipe:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy mpg.csv > displ-hwy-piped.png
file -b displ-hwy-piped.png
```

`-O` overrides that guess. Use `-O ansi` or `-O ascii` to get terminal art
when piping, for example into a pager, or `-O svg`, `-O pdf`, and so on for
another image format:

```bash
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -O ansi mpg.csv | less -R
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -O svg mpg.csv > displ-hwy.svg
```

### `--width` (`-w`), `--height`

In the terminal, the size is in characters. The width defaults to the width
of your terminal:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -O ascii -w 50 --height 15 mpg.csv
```

For images, the size is in `--units` and defaults to 6 by 4 inches:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv -o displ-hwy-wide.png -w 9 --height 3 \
  mpg.csv
```

![](displ-hwy-wide.png){fig-alt="A wide, short version of the scatter plot" width="560"}

### `--units`, `--dpi`

`--units` is one of `in` (the default), `cm`, `mm`, or `px`. `--dpi` sets the
resolution in pixels per inch, which defaults to 300 (print quality). A lower
resolution gives an image with fewer pixels and a smaller file:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -o displ-hwy-small.png \
  -w 10 --height 7 --units cm --dpi 100 mpg.csv
file -b displ-hwy-small.png
```

## Choosing a geom

When both `--x` and `--y` are given, `rush` draws points (`geom_point`):

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg mtcars.csv
```

When only `--x` is given, `rush` draws a histogram for a numeric (or date)
column:

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy mpg.csv
```

and a bar chart for anything else (text, factors, logicals), which counts the
rows per value. For example, the number of cars per class:

```{term}
rush plot -x class mpg.csv
```

To count the distinct values of a numeric column, turn it into a factor:

```{term}
rush plot -x 'factor(cyl)' mtcars.csv
```

The choice between histogram and bar chart is made when the script runs, so
the [generated script](#seeing-the-generated-script) contains
`rush::geom_auto()`.

### `--geom` (`-g`)

Override the guessed geom. Any ggplot2 geom works, without the `geom_` prefix:

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -g density mpg.csv
```

```{term}
rush plot -x class -y hwy -g boxplot mpg.csv
```

Some geoms show more detail as an image, such as the confidence band of
`smooth`:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -g smooth -o smooth.png mpg.csv
```

![](smooth.png){fig-alt="A smoothed curve of highway mileage against engine displacement, with a gray confidence band" width="560"}

### `--geom-args`

Pass arguments to the geom, as R code. For example, `adjust` smooths a density
curve, and `alpha` makes it transparent:

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -f drv -g density --geom-args 'adjust = 2, alpha = 0.5' \
  -n mpg.csv | grep 'ggplot('
```

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -f drv -g density --geom-args 'adjust = 2, alpha = 0.5' \
  -o density.png mpg.csv
```

![](density.png){fig-alt="Smoothed, half-transparent density curves of highway mileage for each drive type in the mpg data set" width="560"}

Arguments set fixed values for the whole layer, unlike aesthetics such as
`--alpha`, which map a column. They also work with the guessed geom, e.g.
`--geom-args 'bins = 20'` for a histogram.

## Aesthetics

Aesthetics map a column to a visual property. Each option takes a column
name, or an R expression such as `'factor(cyl)'` or `'hwy / cty'`.

### `--color` (`-c`)

Map a column to color. A discrete column gets a color per value:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c class -o color.png mpg.csv
```

![](color.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of highway mileage against engine displacement, with a different color for each of the seven car classes" width="560"}

### `--fill` (`-f`)

Map a column to the fill color of areas, such as bars, histograms, and
density curves. In a bar chart, it stacks the counts of each group:

```{term}
rush plot -x class -f drv mpg.csv
```

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -f drv -o fill.png mpg.csv
```

![](fill.png){fig-alt="Stacked histogram of highway mileage, with a different fill color for each drive type" width="560"}

### `--alpha` (`-a`)

Map a column to transparency:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy --alpha cty -o alpha.png mpg.csv
```

![](alpha.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of highway mileage against engine displacement, where cars with a higher city mileage are drawn more opaque" width="560"}

To make the whole geom semi-transparent, use `--geom-args 'alpha = 0.5'`
instead. A constant such as `--alpha 0.5` is mapped as if it were a column,
so it adds a legend.

### `--size`

Map a column to the size of points, which gives a bubble chart:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --size hp -c 'factor(cyl)' -o size.png mtcars.csv
```

![](size.png){fig-alt="Bubble chart of fuel economy against weight, where heavier engines have bigger bubbles, colored by the number of cylinders" width="560"}

### `--shape`

Map a discrete column to the shape of points (ggplot2 can't map a numeric
column to shape, so wrap it in `factor()`):

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy --shape drv -o shape.png mpg.csv
```

![](shape.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of highway mileage against engine displacement, with circles, triangles, and squares for the three drive types" width="560"}

### `--group`

Group the rows, for geoms such as `line` that connect them. Here, each of the
five economic indicators (scaled from 0 to 1) gets its own line:

```{term}
rush plot -x date -y value01 --group variable -g line economics.csv
```

`--color`, `--fill`, `--shape`, and other discrete aesthetics group the rows
too; use `--group` to get separate lines without separate colors.

### `--z`

Map a column to `z`, for geoms that draw a third variable on the plane, such as
`contour`. ggplot2's `faithfuld` data set has the density of eruptions of the
Old Faithful geyser:

```{term}
rush plot -x waiting -y eruptions -z density -g contour \
  -o contour.png faithfuld.csv
```

![](contour.png){fig-alt="Contour lines of the density of Old Faithful eruptions by waiting time and eruption duration" width="560"}

### `--aes`

Map any other aesthetic with `key=value` pairs, separated by commas. For
example, `label` for `text` (the `--geom-args` keep the labels inside the plot
and drop the ones that would overlap):

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --aes 'label=model' -g text -o label.png \
  --geom-args 'hjust = "inward", check_overlap = TRUE' mtcars.csv
```

![](label.png){fig-alt="The names of the cars in mtcars, placed by weight and fuel economy" width="560"}

## Scales and labels

### `--log`

Log-transform the `x` axis, the `y` axis, or both (`xy`):

```{term}
rush plot -x hp -y mpg --log x mtcars.csv
```

### `--title`, `--xlab`, `--ylab`

Add a title and axis labels. They default to nothing and the column names:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --title 'Heavier cars use more fuel' \
  --xlab 'Weight (1000 lbs)' --ylab 'Miles per gallon' \
  -o labels.png mtcars.csv
```

![](labels.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of fuel economy against weight, with the title 'Heavier cars use more fuel' and descriptive axis labels" width="560"}

## Facets

### `--facets`

Split the plot into small multiples. A one-sided formula such as `'~ class'`
wraps the panels
([`facet_wrap()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/facet_wrap.html)):

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy --facets '~ class' -o facets.png mpg.csv
```

![](facets.png){fig-alt="Seven small scatter plots of highway mileage against engine displacement, one per car class" width="560"}

A two-sided formula such as `'drv ~ cyl'` puts the panels in a grid, with rows
and columns
([`facet_grid()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/facet_grid.html)).

### `--margins`

Add a panel with all rows to each row and column of a grid:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy --facets 'drv ~ cyl' --margins mpg.csv
```

## Customizing with R code

### `--pre`

Run R code before the plot is built, to transform `df`. For example, plot the
average fuel economy per number of cylinders:

```{term}
rush plot -x cyl -y avg_mpg -g col \
  --pre 'df <- dplyr::summarise(df, avg_mpg = mean(mpg), .by = cyl)' \
  mtcars.csv
```

### `--post`

Run R code after the plot is built, to add layers, scales, or a theme. The
plot is available as `p`, and the value of the last expression is drawn.
ggplot2 is loaded, so its functions don't need the `ggplot2::` prefix:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -o post.png \
  --post 'p + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + theme_minimal()' mtcars.csv
```

![](post.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of fuel economy against weight with a linear regression line and a minimal theme" width="560"}

## Input

### Files

`plot` reads the same [formats](../formats.qmd) as `rush run`, such as CSV,
Parquet, Excel, and DuckDB. The format follows from the extension, or set it
with `--input-format` (`-F`).

### Standard input

With `-` as the file, `plot` reads from standard input, so it can be the last
step of a [pipeline](../pipelines.qmd). Without a file, `plot` is an error; it
doesn't read standard input unless you ask for it:

```{term}
rush run 'dplyr::filter(df, class == "suv")' mpg.csv |
  rush plot -x displ -y hwy -O ascii -
```

### Multiple files

With multiple files, each is read into the list `dfs`, and only the first into
`df`. Use `--pre` to combine them into `df`:

```{term}
rush run -o compact.csv 'dplyr::filter(df, class == "compact")' mpg.csv
rush run -o suv.csv 'dplyr::filter(df, class == "suv")' mpg.csv
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c class --pre 'df <- dplyr::bind_rows(dfs)' \
  compact.csv suv.csv
```

## Seeing the generated script

`rush plot` writes an R script and runs it. `--dry-run` (`-n`) prints that
script instead, so you can see the ggplot2 code, or save it and build on it:

```{term}
rush plot -x displ -y hwy -c drv -n mpg.csv
```

Add `--no-rush` (`-R`) for a script that doesn't need rush to run. See
[Scripts](../scripts.qmd) for more.

## Help

```{term}
rush plot -h
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv mpg.csv economics.csv faithfuld.csv compact.csv suv.csv
```
